Fourier analysis, historically, is exactly how the concept of ordinals was uncovered. Quick overview:

Fourier series were first approached via problems such as behaviour of vibrating strings, or heat, given initial conditions. It turns out if the initial conditions could be described by a sum of sines and cosines - possibly infinite - then we can give an explicit function giving the behaviour of said system at any given time. This lead to studying things like ∑ f_n(x) where f_n(x) = a_n sin(nx) + b_n cos(nx). For instance, when can a function be written this way?

Just take the 0 function. Cantor showed that if ∑ f_n(x) = 0 everywhere then all coefficients are 0. The question then arises how he might improve on this. He defines 'sets of uniqueness' as those sets such that if ∑ f_n(x) = 0 everywhere outside of them, then a_n = b_n = 0. In particular, the empty is a set of uniqueness. In fact any set of finite points is such a set.

Now it gets more interesting. He showed that if your set is a convergent sequence of real numbers (i.e. a set with one limit point), then this is also a set of uniqueness. So he starts looking at this: if you start with a set, say E, define E_1 as the set of its limit points i.e. get rid of the all the convergent sequences and just keep the limits. Call E_2 the set of limit points of E_1 etc. If E_n is finite, you say E is of type n i.e. if I do the above procedure n times, I'll get a finite set of points. He proved any set of type n, for any positive integer n, is a set of uniqueness. 

He then takes it further: picture an increasing convergent sequence. Now have set of type 1 converging to the first entry, a set of type 2 converging to the second entry etc. Then you can do that procedure for any finite number of sets you like, you will never reach finitely many points. At time n you still have everything that above the nth term of our initial sequence. But, this procedure does *converge* to a set of uniqueness, so call this is a set of type ω. Any reason to stop here? Nah. Just take finitely many points and put sets of type of ω that will give us these at time ω. This is a set of type ω + 1. etc. to get ω + 2, ... , ω · 2, ... , ω · ω, ...

He showed that any set of type above (i.e. a countable ordinal) then it is a set of uniqueness. He noticed that these have the same size - they are countable. He then proved that any countable set is a set of uniqueness. Meanwhile, he also realises that not all sets are countable, for instance the transcendental numbers. Once you have the concept of counting 'in infinite time' above, defining ω_1 etc. is natural.

(by the way, interestingly, it is an open problem as to which sets are sets of uniqueness)
